objectives: Define heat as transfer of energy.
Distinguish heat, internal energy and temperature, and apply energy conservation to heat exchange.

misconceptions.claim: Heat flows from a cold body to a hot one.
misconceptions.correction: Heat flows from the hotter body to the colder one, until they reach the same temperature.

authored_exercises.stem: In which direction does heat flow when a hot body touches a cold body?
authored_exercises.answer: From the hot body to the cold body.
solution: Heat flows because of the temperature difference.
The direction is from higher temperature to lower temperature.
It continues until both reach the same temperature.

authored_exercises.stem: What is true about the temperatures of two bodies when they reach thermal equilibrium?
solution: Thermal equilibrium means no net heat flows between the bodies.
That happens when their temperatures are the same.
The temperatures do not have to equal the surroundings.

sections.title: Temperature Change and Heat Capacity
objectives: Observe heat transfer and change in temperature and mass.
Calculate final temperature after heat transfer between two objects.

misconceptions.claim: A larger temperature change always means more heat was transferred.
misconceptions.correction: The heat also depends on the mass and the specific heat capacity. A small metal block can change temperature a lot while absorbing less heat than a large tank of water that changes only slightly.
misconceptions.signal: Temperature change alone does not determine heat.

sections.title: Phase Change and Latent Heat
objectives: Calculate final temperature from heat transfer.

misconceptions.claim: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon in the same pot of soup reach the same temperature at the same rate.
misconceptions.correction: The metal conducts the heat away far faster, so it feels hotter long before the wooden one does.

misconceptions.claim: The temperature of a liquid rises steadily while it boils away.
misconceptions.correction: It stays at the boiling point until the liquid has gone. The heat supplied goes into the latent heat of vaporisation, breaking the bonds between molecules rather than raising the temperature.

sections.title: Heat Transfer Methods
objectives: Discuss the different methods of heat transfer.
Compare conduction, convection and radiation, and identify the dominant mechanism in a given situation.

misconceptions.claim: Heat cannot be transferred without a material medium.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation carries energy through a vacuum as electromagnetic waves. That is how the Sun’s energy reaches the Earth.
misconceptions.signal: Conduction and convection need a medium; radiation does not.

authored_exercises.stem: Name the three methods of heat transfer.
solution: Conduction transfers heat by particle collisions without bulk motion.
Convection transfers heat by the bulk movement of a fluid.
Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves.

authored_exercises.stem: Which method of heat transfer can carry energy through a vacuum?
solution: Radiation is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium.
That is how energy reaches the Earth from the Sun.

authored_exercises.stem: A metal rod is heated at one end. By which method does heat reach the other end? Explain.
authored_exercises.answer: Conduction, by collisions and vibrations passing energy along the rod without the metal itself moving.
solution: The heated particles vibrate more strongly.
They collide with neighbouring particles and pass energy along.
The metal does not flow, so the transfer is conduction.

objectives: Observe conduction of heat in collisions.

misconceptions.claim: Conduction is the transfer of heat by the movement of the heated substance.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction is by collisions between neighbouring particles, without the substance moving. The bulk movement of a heated fluid is convection, which is a different mechanism.

misconceptions.claim: Hot air sinks because heat makes things heavier.
misconceptions.correction: Heating a gas makes it expand and become less dense, so buoyancy pushes it upward. Cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place.
misconceptions.signal: Convection currents rise from the hot region and sink from the cold region.

misconceptions.claim: Objects emit thermal radiation only when they are visibly hot.
misconceptions.correction: Every object above absolute zero emits infrared radiation. A hotter object emits more power and at shorter wavelengths.

sec-6:exr-29.stem: A student measures the rate of heat conduction through the walls of a container holding melting ice, using $Q/t=kA(T_{2}-T_{1})/d$. The container is kept in a room warmer than 0°C, and the student wants the ice to melt in a shorter time. Which change should the student make?
solution: The heat needed to melt the ice is $Q=mL_{f}$, so a smaller mass $m$ needs less heat and melts sooner.
Increasing the wall thickness $d$, reducing the surface area $A$, or lowering the outside temperature $T_{2}$ all reduce the rate of heat transfer and make the melting take longer.
sec-6:exr-29.solution_provenance: OpenStax CNXML solution element (in file); the stem is rewritten so the experiment is described in the question instead of a figure

sec-3:we-ex-8.answer: (a) about 90 kJ (b) about 30% to the pan (c) about 70% to the water
steps: A 0.500-kg aluminum pan holds 0.250 L (0.250 kg) of water, and both are heated from 20.0°C to 80.0°C.
The pan takes $2.70/8.98=30%$ and the water takes $6.28/8.98=70%$ of the heat.
The brakes retain 10%, so $Q=7.35×10^{5}J$ enters 100 kg of brake material.
The brakes heat by about 9.2°C, which is why a long descent can overheat them.
The hot aluminum pan loses heat and the cold water gains it: $m_{pan}c_{Al}(150-T)=m_{w}c_{w}(T-20.0)$ .
The final temperature is much closer to the water's initial temperature because water has the larger specific heat capacity.

sec-4:we-exr-30.answer: Snow remains at 0°C while it melts because the heat from the warmer air goes into the latent heat of fusion, not into raising the temperature. The process is slow because a large amount of heat is needed for the phase change.
steps: Snow is ice at 0°C. Heat arriving from the warmer air first goes into melting the ice, not into raising its temperature.
The latent heat of fusion of water is large, about $334kJ/kg$, so melting a significant depth of snow takes a long time.
While ice and liquid water coexist, the mixture stays at 0°C. Only after all the ice has melted can the meltwater warm above freezing.

sec-6:we-ex-10.answer: about 3.4 kg of ice melts in one day
steps: Styrofoam has $k≈0.010J/(s\cdot m\cdot °C)$. The conduction rate is $Q/t=kA(T_{2}-T_{1})/d$ .
The heat rate is the rate needed to evaporate 1.00 g/s: $Q/t=mL_{v}/t=(1.00×10^{-3})(2.26×10^{6})/1=2.26×10^{3}W$ .
The bottom of the pan is only about 5°C hotter than the boiling water, which shows how effective aluminum is as a conductor.
With air density $1.29kg/m^{3}$, the mass is $m=(1.29)(648)=836kg$ .
About 4.6 kW of heating is needed to warm the incoming air.
The body loses energy by evaporation at $P=120W$ .
The person loses about 100 W by radiation, which is comparable to the 125 W produced at rest.
The radiated power is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature: $P∝T^{4}$ .
The radiated power therefore rises by about 30%.
